newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Ousted Kazakh c. banker to boost securities trade.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Kazakh c. banker to boost securities trade.

text.p: Ousted reformist central banker Grigory Marchenko has vowed to fire up a dormant securities market in his new job in Kazakhstan's National Securities Commission, but admits the new position gives him far less power.

Grigory Marchenko, rebutting investor alarm in an interview with Reuters late on Monday, said he viewed his appointment as chairman of the commission as a sign the government wanted the securities body to become as successful as the central bank.

"Maybe I have less power than I had," said Marchenko, ousted by President Nursultan Nazarbayev last week. "But I feel the government wants us to replicate in securities the successes we've had...at the national bank."

Western investors had viewed Marchenko, 37, as the main guarantor of economic stability in the oil-rich former Soviet republic and news of his removal from the national bank rang alarm bells in Almaty's expatriate community.
"Everybody looks at his new job as a marginalisation," said one Western observer in Almaty.

Marchenko had cut a high profile among foreign investors, many of whom said his grasp of economics and fluent English, both learned at Moscow's elite Institute for International Relations, made for swifter business.

Marchenko has been closely involved in Kazakhstan's debut Eurobond issue -- to be placed next month -- and in regulating the market in government Treasury Bills and taking tough decisions to reform the country's troubled banking sector.
Some feared Marchenko, who once described his job of closing failed banks as that of an "undertaker", could catch a bullet from a disgruntled bank's hitman.
Pleased at all the fuss, Marchenko looked full of energy at the Commission on Monday where breathless aides ran in and out of his office every ten minutes.
He said the securities market and pension funds, both of which he has been asked to reform, were inextricably linked.
"As private pension funds grow, they have to be able to invest in capital markets," Marchenko said.
He said Kazakhstan's sluggish privatisation programme was crucial to the success of both sectors.
The vast, Central Asian nation of 16.9 million has potentially rich privatisation pickings in the energy, mining and metallurgical sectors.

"Privatisation is part of the programme I discussed with the prime minister (Akezhan Kazhegeldin)," said Marchenko. "So far I've had support to try to channel privatised enterprises into the corporate market."
He said he aimed to create a market of "blue-chip" companies ready to trade by May next year.
"The next six months will see institutional and technical preparations and proper audits for our potential blue-chips," Marchenko said, adding these would help to "kick-start" the market.

Kazhegeldin said earlier this month that foreign consultants from Banque Paribas, Merrill Lynch investment bank, accountants Price Waterhouse and other firms would make the tender process more transparent.

Marchenko said he would travel with a roadshow to promote Kazakhstan's planned $100 million three-year eurobond -- aimed at putting Kazakhstan on the international financial map -- in London, Geneva and New York at the beginning of December.
Kazakhstan secured a Ba3 long-term rating for foreign currency bonds, and BB- ratings from both Standard and Poor's and London-based IBCA.
"I think the ratings were acceptable at this stage because we're newcomers to the international market," Marchenko said.
